prize_parts.citation: for a poetic oeuvre that has remade Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and a sustained critical dialogue with inherited forms

statement.case_for: My first choice is unchanged: Adonis, on literary grounds. The case is formal and linguistic achievement over a very long body of work. Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses, as I know them from public accounts and translated selections, work on the Arabic poetic language itself through mythic personae, fragmentation and a critical dialogue with the classical tradition. The voice is distinctive, the project has been sustained for decades, and the poetry and the poetics are linked in a way that gives the whole oeuvre coherence. The citation should rest on the poetry alone. The essays may show how coherent the project is, but they should not carry a separate claim. His public and political roles do not enter my assessment. The age of the oeuvre is not a literary criterion either, and I give it no weight. I have not independently verified any of this and rely on public knowledge and the longlist description. What did change in this round is the order of my alternatives. In round 1 I listed Carson first. Palm's argument that the Cărtărescu case rests on the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, where the architecture is the point, answers part of my own evenness doubt. That claim can be tested on the major works without a verdict on every volume. I now name Cărtărescu as my first alternative and Carson as my second. This is a modest change in weighting, not a change of first choice. I have not moved him above Adonis, because I still cannot confirm the evenness of the late novels from the evidence supplied.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation against my own choice is assessability. The force of Adonis lies in Arabic prosody, diction and allusion to inherited forms, and the committee can judge these only through translations and secondhand accounts. Sward and Sem-Sandberg are right that this makes my claim about the later poetry weaker than my claim about the early and middle collections. If the later volumes cannot be shown to hold the level of the major collections, the whole-oeuvre claim narrows. In that case Cărtărescu, where the load-bearing works are few and large, or Carson, whose English text is directly legible to the committee, would present a case that is easier to examine. I also accept that my weighting is contestable. I rate sustained transformation of a poetic language above imaginative scale or reconfiguration of genre, and the committee has to argue that distinction openly rather than treat it as settled.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and argues that the case rests on the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, where the architecture is the point. She holds that uneven quality in some volumes is a question about sustained quality that can be tested against the major works, and that translation loss is a separate question of whether the achievement can be seen at all.
responses.response: This distinction is useful, and it is the main reason I moved Cărtărescu up to my first alternative. A case that rests on identifiable major works can be tested, and my round-1 doubt about evenness weighs less on a claim of that shape. I would apply the same test to my own candidate, which means naming the Adonis collections that carry the claim and asking whether the later poetry matches them. I still part from you on the weight of translation. You treat it as a problem that applies equally to every candidate, and I agree. But on that standard it also stands against the claim that prose built on structure is safe, since density and rhythm are what translation distorts. Neither of us can verify that, and I would not let it decide the ranking in either direction.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson first, arguing that her voice and formal reinvention are directly legible in English, that the concerns of grief, desire and the fragment recur across her forms, and that the case for Adonis is less secure because Arabic prosody reaches the committee only through intermediaries.
responses.response: Your point about legibility is the strongest argument against my own ranking, and I do not dispute it. The Carson claim can be tested on the page by the whole committee, and mine cannot. I would answer on two points. First, being hard to assess is a limit on our evidence, not a measure of the achievement, so the right remedy is better evidence, such as readings from Arabic-language experts, and not a lower rank for the poet. Second, the scope question you raise for Carson applies here too. A citation for her has to stay with her own lyric and essayistic writing, and one for Adonis has to stay with the poetry. Your continuity argument across her forms is persuasive on development. I still weigh a sustained transformation of a literary language somewhat above a sustained reconfiguration of genre, and I hold that as a judgment, not as a finding.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis fifth. She accepts that his formal and linguistic achievement is among the clearest on the list, but is cautious about ranking a poet first on translated selections alone, and says influence on later poets does not prove literary merit.
responses.response: I accept both cautions. Influence on later poets does not enter my case. The case is what the poems do with the language, and I have said so. On translated selections, your caution is fair and the committee should state it plainly. I would add that the same caution applies to a first-place ranking for any candidate whose strongest qualities lie in the original, including a Romanian prose stylist. If you would not rank Adonis first without Arabic-language readers, I would ask whether you apply the same standard to Cărtărescu. We may differ on that, but the standard should be common. I would also welcome your account of what you think the translated poetry does and does not carry, since you have read it as a prose critic and not as a poet.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first, but says he would move toward Carson or Adonis if the evidence for sustained quality beyond the best-known volumes proved thin. He also argues that Cărtărescu's translation problem is less total than that of Arabic verse, because much of his force lies in imagery, structure and scale.
responses.response: Your conditional is the honest form of this case, and I take it as a shared test. The case for Cărtărescu is more convincing to me when it is stated as a claim about the trilogy and Solenoid, with the poetry and early fiction treated as unassessed. On translation, I do not think imagery and structure are exempt from loss. The sentence-level patterning that you and Mattson both describe as distinctive is the first thing a translator has to give up. I would not place his translation problem at less than total. I would place it at unknown for him and for Adonis alike, and I would ask the committee to treat both under one standard.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis second. She says my ordering is open to question if the committee gives priority to the transformation of a literary language, and she argues that a prose project built on large-scale structure is somewhat less exposed to translation loss than verse resting on prosody.
responses.response: I agree that the order depends on how the committee weighs transformation of a language against imaginative architecture, and I think that is the actual dispute, more than the question of evenness. We differ on exposure to translation loss. You state your judgment as unverified, and I accept that. I read the evidence as symmetric, and I would not let an assumption of lower exposure raise one candidate over the other. Your point that the Adonis case rests on prosody you cannot assess in the original is also true of me. I would propose that the committee settle this by seeking outside readings, not by assuming that one genre translates better.

uncertainties: How well Arabic prosody, diction and allusion survive in the available translations, and whether the committee can judge this without independent expert readings. I have not verified any translation.
Whether the later poetry of Adonis holds the level of the major earlier collections. My knowledge of it is incomplete and I cannot settle it from the supplied evidence.
Whether the late, very long novels of Cărtărescu are evenly sustained. This bears directly on whether he should rank above Adonis, and I cannot test it.

Whether the committee could obtain outside readings of the Arabic and Romanian originals. Profile material records a stated practice of seeking international expert reports for literatures where it lacks deep competence, but I do not know what exists for these candidates and make no claim about it.
How to word a citation for Carson that rests on her own lyric and essayistic writing while excluding translations, classical scholarship and book-object form.
Whether a common standard for translation uncertainty can be agreed. Members assume different degrees of exposure for prose and verse, and none of us can verify the assumptions.

I rely on public knowledge and the longlist descriptions without independent verification. Carlberg's simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and this stage models a committee recommendation, not the Academy's decision.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1: none apparent from the supplied profile that requires recusal. My scholarly work on modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature and translation (including Celan) is context only and does not show a preference for any candidate. I disclose that I am the chair and the only member whose first preference is B007, and that I wrote the round-1 chair summary. The questions in that summary were meant to test every leading position, mine included, and I have applied the same tests to my own case here. The profile records no personal, professional or archival tie between me and any shortlisted writer. Ceremony speeches given on behalf of the Academy are collective statements and are not evidence of my vote.
